concept.name: Volga
concept.definition: Volga (vomma) is the second-order sensitivity of an option's value to volatility: the rate of change of vega per unit change in implied volatility. It measures vega convexity — how a position's volatility exposure itself grows or shrinks as volatility moves.
concept.intuition: Volga is to vega what gamma is to delta: a long-volga position becomes more long volatility as volatility rises and less as it falls, so it benefits from volatility of volatility.
concept.mechanics: Volga = d(vega)/d(sigma) = d2V/d(sigma)2. Volga is positive for long options away from the money and peaks for OTM/wing options, which is why strangles and wings carry volga while ATM options carry little. Vega-neutral books built from different strikes can still be net long or short volga.
concept.formula: Volga = d2V/d(sigma)2; Black-Scholes: Volga = Vega * (d1 * d2) / sigma.
concept.failure_modes: Volga exposure hides in strike-diversified books that report flat vega: a volatility spike re-prices the wings far more than first-order vega predicts. Because volga lives in OTM options, it is entangled with skew dynamics that a single-volatility model cannot represent.
concept.misconceptions: Being vega-neutral is not being volatility-neutral: volga (and vanna) leave residual exposure to volatility changes. Volga also is not 'the volatility of volatility' itself — it is a price sensitivity to that second-order risk.
concept.example: A vega-flat book long far-OTM wings and short ATM options has positive volga: when implied volatility jumps from 15% to 25%, the wings' vega inflates and the book gains beyond what its zero initial vega implied.
